wa_a_servant_to_liberty.notes: Shared start with Freedom or Death: face and crack climbing up a slab to a bolted belay. Locate the correct start among the East Face cluster of routes, not Liberty Crack or Thin Red Line.
Follow bolts up and slightly left/right on sustained face climbing, per the shared Freedom or Death line.
Last pitch shared with Freedom or Death; from here A Servant to Liberty breaks right to join Thin Red Line just below its 3rd-pitch anchor rather than continuing up Freedom or Death.
Starts up easy terrain to a right-leaning overlap with tricky liebacks and smeary feet, the first of the route's new East Face pitches.
Traverses left to flake laybacks protected by two small cams, then stems over a roof and steps right around an arete to the anchor.
Climbs a shallow corner then steps right around a rounded arete on classic golden-granite edges, with a big move back left to a hand rail.
A 165-ft bolted mega-slab with 14 bolts and four cruxy sequences; a 0.75 cam is needed after the second bolt for extra protection.
The route's crux slab pitch: technical, thin edges ('razor blades') and funky foot moves on deteriorating rock that eases to 5.10- near the top.
Varied, unexpectedly fun 5.10 climbing on decent rock; a #3 cam protects a left-facing corner and small cams cover the final arete traverse.
Short crack past loose blocks; a single bolt lets you avoid a 'kitty litter' loose block on an exposed traverse.
Low-angle left-facing corner with finger cracks protected by nuts, wandering to low-angle terrain and a fixed nut anchor above the trees.

wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.notes: Low-angle, sometimes water-polished slab at 5.4-5.8, with runouts that can be long but on easy ground. The first two pitches link in one lead, and a competent party can run the next three and a half as a running belay to the top of the lower slabs. The pitch that reaches the first big ledge can be wet; a ramp on the left avoids it. P7 climbs a short 5.7 wall before easing back to slab. The whole route follows a gully slab, so anything knocked off above funnels straight down these pitches — the many bent hangers show it; do not linger below other parties.

A fun blocky ramp cutting through the steeper wall above the lower slabs, a full rope length from the base of that wall. Protection is sparse — two bolts of 5.7-5.8 at the start, a bolt about halfway and a fixed pin about 15 ft below the belay — but the climbing is easy. On the way down this ramp is downclimbed rather than rappelled.
The first 5.9 pitch, on steeper rock where the bolts are closer together as the moves get harder. It ends on a large ledge.

wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.belay: Walk past the chained stop to the foot of the steep wall on the left and belay on a flake just under the next pitch's bolt line.
wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.notes: Easy climbing above the ledge. Skip the chain anchors and scramble to the foot of the steep wall to the left, belaying on a flake below the bolt line of the next pitch.
The first 5.10 pitch: well-bolted, balancy face climbing that is a fair test for the upper crux. Stay on the bolt line; forcing moves off it makes the pitch harder.
A more moderate pitch (roughly 5.8) up to chains. The top of this pitch makes a worthwhile objective on its own; above it the rock and climbing are poorer.

Easy (about 5.0-5.8) but the most runout section, on fair, slightly polished rock that sheds stones onto parties below. P13 is a full rope length with small cams useful in flakes, and can be run as one lead to a second set of chains up and right. A moderate pitch with five or six bolts follows to a belay where the wall kicks back. P15's two bolts are easy to miss and P16-17 have only the stations. Where the wall kicks back, go left to a bolt, up and right to a belay between a stand of trees and a heather patch (about 40 m, two bolts), then right along an obvious ramp of roughly 120 ft to the headwall; the trees and heather are useful landmarks on the descent too. Parties most often get lost here.
The first pitch of the upper headwall, where the bolt line picks back up, finishing on a tricky friction slab (around 5.9).

The crux: a steep, sustained wall nearly a full 60 m rope length, needing around 17 draws (bring long ones or back-clean). Its anchor has no chains; a chained station about 10 m higher lets two 60 m ropes reach the base of this pitch on the descent.
A chimney climbed by stemming and scrounging; it is often wet and can feel harder than the crux late in the day. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.
An easier, fun pitch up blocky ground, ending about 30 m below the summit.
A steep friction finish to the summit that looks easy from the belay but has few holds; well bolted and airy. Grades given for it range from 5.9 to 5.10a.

ca_aiguille_extra_east_buttress.notes: Begin in the corner below an orange panel facing east, where the buttress meets the ground. Climb a blocky weakness, make a strenuous move left to a dihedral on the lowest pillar, and follow a hand crack to a belay on a nice ledge atop the pillar. This is part of the three-pitch direct start that replaces the original first two pitches (5.6 and 5.8).

The physical and mental crux. Step left around the corner from the belay into a dihedral with blocks, make a bouldery move to a rail sticking out about a foot with a flake above it, then work left past an edge and traverse the face to a belay in the wide crack that splits the lower buttress. Sporty, gear-protected, with a serious feel.

Climb the steep splitter for about 35 m, step right to an obvious ledge, then follow a less strenuous corner to a pedestal at the top of the pillar with a large diving-board block. The belay takes medium nuts.

Pass a wide stretch and a ledge to reach the steep crack leaning right, sustained hands to fists, passing an old homemade hanger in the wall to the right of the crack. Follow the crack to its end, trend right over blocky terrain, and belay in blocks in the middle of the buttress. Aid on the first ascent.
Head up and left to a corner crack capped by a block that forms a keyhole. Belay under the block.
Go about 5 m left from the belay into a chimney system and make wide moves to a blocky exit onto the bivy ledge used by the first ascent party.

Several options leave the bivy ledge: a splitter crack on the left, a dihedral center-right, or a broken crack system trending right. The right option goes through a small roof to blocky terrain below the upper headwall. With a 70 m rope belay at the headwall base; with a 60 m rope belay short and scramble about 10 m of easy third class to the base.

The showpiece. Start in the perfect hand crack to the right of the off-width splitter. It widens a bit, then pinches to tight hands and ring locks before the wide crack joins it from the left. Bold moves reach a ledge with an old angle piton of doubtful quality; a #6 cam makes a convenient belay, otherwise use small gear and chockstones.

A flaky layback leads to small footholds, then a 10 m traverse right to a good vertical hand crack. Follow it to blocky terrain and belay in a corner at large blocks. Steep and bouldery in the dihedral, with excellent movement; aided at A2 originally. A second source rates it 5.10+ while the original route description gives 5.9, so treat the grade as a range.
Climb the short steep corner and the broken face just left of it to blocky, easier terrain that tops out the Aiguille. Walk off.
